performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: A trumpet call cuts across the strings’ restless A-minor figure. Between the scherzo’s two fast spans, Bruckner gives the violins a broad F-major tune — with the trumpet’s rhythm still quietly haunting it.

sections.label: A · Trumpet calls above restless strings
sections.mNote: An octave leap and repeated notes drive the A-minor scherzo

sections.label: B · Winds answer the quiet strings
sections.mNote: The short figures change hands and turn upside down

sections.label: C · A violin song in F major
sections.mNote: Soft timpani introduce the slower trio

sections.label: A · The trumpet call returns
sections.mNote: The opening string figure restarts at the original fast tempo

sections.mNote: Repeated figures drive towards the final chord

relations.label: The scherzo returns after the trio
relations.basis: The score’s da capo restores the scherzo after its F-major trio. The 326 s measured offset agrees with the opening and the return marked near 328 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.973, sustained 195.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 326 s (cache/form/bruckner-7-scherzo.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A trumpet above busy strings
cues.text: The strings repeat a compact A-minor figure. After four bars, a solo trumpet enters with an octave leap and a sharply pointed rhythm; clarinet answers. The string figure keeps going underneath, ready to carry the call into the whole orchestra.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), III, opening, printed p. 51. The four-bar string introduction is also described by the Munich analysis: https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The same notes, turned over
cues.text: The strings resume quietly and the winds answer in longer phrases. Bruckner turns the short figures upside down and passes them between high and low instruments. The tiny scraps that fed the opening uproar now sustain an intricate, softer conversation.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, letter D, p. 57. Inversions in the scherzo’s contrasting section are illustrated in the Munich analysis cited above.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A drumbeat before the violin song
cues.text: Soft timpani introduce the trio. First violins begin a long F-major melody, marked gesangvoll — songful — over a held bass. The tempo is slower, but the trumpet’s pointed rhythm returns among these gentler phrases.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, Trio, p. 66: Etwas langsamer, timpani introduction, gesangvoll violins, F pedal and trumpet entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fire across the street
cues.text: On 8 December 1881, Vienna’s Ringtheater burns across the street from Bruckner’s home. Afraid the fire will spread, he gathers his manuscripts. The following day he sees the bodies of victims being carried away. He describes the disaster in a letter to his brother-in-law.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs relates the Ringtheater fire, Bruckner’s response and his letter to Johann Baptist Hueber the following Sunday. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: The fast strings start again
cues.text: The trio ends in F major. After the pause, the quick A-minor string figure returns, followed by the trumpet call. Bruckner asks for the whole scherzo again: its quiet wind exchanges and great brass entries belong to the return as surely as the opening tune.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, end of Trio, p. 70: Scherzo Da Capo; return to p. 51.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Leipzig welcomes the Seventh
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch conducts the Seventh’s premiere in Leipzig on 30 December 1884. Bruckner is sixty. After years of bruising receptions for his symphonies, this performance with the Gewandhaus Orchestra gives him a public triumph.
cues.evidence: Premiere and reception: Thomas May, St. Louis Symphony, https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/; Berlin Philharmonic, https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/

cues.title: The short figure fills the orchestra
cues.text: The strings’ repeated figure gathers woodwind and brass around it. Trumpets press the opening rhythm forward, and trombones, tuba and timpani reinforce the final climb. The scherzo ends in A minor with the whole orchestra striking together.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, final pages of the scherzo, pp. 60–65, repeated after the Trio.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A soft drumbeat opens the trio
transitions.from: B · Winds answer the quiet strings
transitions.to: C · A violin song in F major
transitions.how: The scherzo closes with the full orchestra in A minor. After the rests, the timpani begin alone and quietly at the slower Etwas langsamer. First violins enter with the F-major trio melody, marked gesangvoll, over sustained inner strings, moving cellos and a held F in the basses.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), III, scherzo ending and Trio opening, pp. 65–66.

transitions.title: F major rests; A minor restarts
transitions.from: C · A violin song in F major
transitions.how: Flute, oboe and clarinet finish the trio above held F-major strings, with the horn quietly recalling the scherzo’s rhythm. The phrase dwindles to pianissimo and stops. Scherzo Da Capo restores the fast A-minor string figure, then the solo trumpet’s octave call.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, Trio ending, p. 70, and scherzo opening, p. 51.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: III. Scherzo, printed pp. 51–65; Trio, pp. 66–70. Scherzo Da Capo returns to the opening.

timeline.note: All five string groups repeat the quiet A-minor figure.
A solo trumpet gives the octave call; clarinet answers above the strings.
Woodwinds and horns join in a crescendo; trumpets rest.
Tutti fortissimo: brass, tuba and a timpani roll over rushing strings.
Softer: flute, oboe and clarinet melody, with horn and trumpet solos over strings.
A soft brass chorale: trombones and tuba swell with the winds.
Oboe, clarinet, bassoon and horn exchange solos above plucked cellos and basses.
A crescendo builds in winds, horns and trumpets over the strings.
Second tutti at fortissimo with trombones, tuba and timpani.
Mezzo-forte wind and horn phrases with a trumpet solo; trombones and timpani rest.
Final build: trombones, tuba and timpani rejoin; fortissimo to the end of the scherzo.
Soft timpani introduce the trio; first violins begin their song over a held bass F.
Horn and trumpet solos over the strings.
Flute, oboe and clarinet take the melody over strings, with one horn.
A pianissimo brass chorale with soft timpani, strings entering at the close.
The trio swells to forte, brass joining strings and winds, then withdraws.
All five string groups return to the quiet A-minor figure.
The solo trumpet’s octave call returns, answered by clarinet.
Woodwinds and horns join in a crescendo; trumpets rest.
Tutti fortissimo again: brass, tuba and timpani.
Softer wind melody with horn and trumpet solos over strings.
Soft brass chorale swelling with the winds.
Wind and horn solos return above plucked cellos and basses.
The closing drive begins: a crescendo in winds, horns and trumpets.
Second tutti at fortissimo with trombones, tuba and timpani.
Mezzo-forte wind and horn phrases; trombones and timpani rest.
The final build to the closing fortissimo of the whole orchestra.

composer.epithet: He spent half his life learning his trade, then wrote symphonies in which a horn call can grow into a wall of brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner stood before the Vienna Philharmonic to conduct his Third Symphony. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped turn the enormous score into a piano duet. Bruckner was fifty-three, a conservatory professor and an internationally admired organist. In the concert hall he was still having to introduce himself.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing. The heavy-footed country dances in his scherzos had passed through his hands long before he wrote for an orchestra.
